intro/hello: Welcome to optimization: the chapter where a classifier finally learns.
intro/recap: The last chapter built two pieces. First, a score function: multiply an image by the weights W, and get one score per class.
intro/loss: Second, a loss function, which grades those scores with one number: high when the classifier is wrong, low when it is right.
intro/third: This chapter supplies the third piece, optimization: a way to find the weights W that make the loss as small as possible.
intro/objective: Written out, the loss is an average over all N training examples, plus a penalty on the size of the weights.
intro/free: The images X and labels y are fixed. Only W is free to change, so the loss is really a function of W alone.
intro/dials: Picture W as a panel of dials: thirty thousand seven hundred and thirty of them for see-far ten. Every setting gives one loss value.
intro/goal: Training means turning the dials until that number is as low as it will go.
intro/general: Our running example is the SVM loss, but the same procedure will later tune networks with millions of weights.
landscape/land: Here is a picture that helps with everything that follows: the loss as a landscape.
landscape/loc: Every possible weight matrix is a location in it, and the loss is the altitude at that spot.
landscape/low: Training is a search for the lowest point.
landscape/dims: The trouble is, for see-far ten this landscape has thirty thousand seven hundred and thirty directions. Nobody can picture that.
landscape/slice: But we can look at slices. Stand on one weight matrix, and pick a random direction: a matrix of the same shape, used like a compass heading.
landscape/walk: Walk along that straight line, recording the loss at each distance a, and you get an ordinary curve.
landscape/map: Add a second direction, walk a grid in both, and the curve grows into a map, colored by height.
creases/one: Start with the loss of one training example. Its slices are flat floors and straight ramps, meeting at sharp creases.
creases/hinge: Each hinge, the max of zero and something, is either off, which is flat, or on, which is a straight ramp.
creases/all: Now average all three hundred examples. The creases blend into a nearly smooth bowl, with a long, gentle valley floor.
creases/reg: Add the regularization penalty, and the valley closes up into a rounder bowl.
creases/convex: A bowl like this is called convex: a straight line between any two points on it never dips below the surface.
creases/nodips: So a convex function has no misleading little dips. Anywhere you cannot go further downhill is a lowest point.
creases/svm: Every hinge is convex, so is the penalty, and sums of convex functions stay convex: the whole SVM loss is one convex bowl.
creases/nn: Neural networks lose this property, yet the downhill methods of this chapter still work remarkably well on them.
creases/kink: One detail: right on a crease, the slope jumps. We just use the slope from either side, called a subgradient, and nothing breaks.
search/blind: How do you find the bottom of a landscape you cannot see? Picture yourself blindfolded, on a hillside.
search/three: Here are three strategies, from hopeless to good.
search/rs: Strategy one: random search. Try lots of random weight matrices, and keep the best one you find.
search/darts: On the map, that is throwing darts anywhere, and remembering the lowest one.
search/rsacc: On see-far ten, the best of a thousand guesses gets about fifteen and a half percent of test images right. Pure guessing gets ten.
search/ls: Strategy two: random local search. Start somewhere, try a small random step, and keep it only if the loss goes down.
search/foot: Blindfolded, that is poking a foot out in a random direction, and stepping only if the ground there is lower.
search/lsacc: That reaches about twenty one point four percent. Better, but wasteful: most pokes point uphill, and get thrown away.
search/slope: Strategy three: feel the ground under your feet, and step the way it drops most steeply. That direction can be computed: no guessing.
search/race: Now let all three race, one move each per round. Gradient descent walks straight downhill, and gets there first.
search/caveat: To be fair, on a small two dimensional map, a few dozen darts cover the ground well. In thirty thousand dimensions, they cover nothing.
gradient/deriv: That direction comes from the slope. In one dimension, the slope at a point is the derivative: nudge the input a little, and how much does the output move per unit?
gradient/rise: Measure it as rise over run. Step a distance h to the right, see how far the function rose, and divide by h.
gradient/shrink: Now let h shrink toward zero. The line through the two points swings around, and settles onto the tangent.
gradient/six: For x squared at three, it settles on six. With a tiny h, the code prints six point zero zero zero zero one.
gradient/sign: Positive means going right goes up. Negative means going right goes down. And the size says how steeply.
gradient/many: But the loss does not have one input. It has one for every weight.
gradient/partial: So nudge one weight, hold all the others still, and measure the slope. That is a partial derivative, written with a curly d.
gradient/every: Do that for every weight, and collect the slopes. That collection is the gradient: one slope per weight, the same shape as W.
gradient/uphill: Taken together, the gradient is a direction, and a special one: it points the way the loss rises fastest.
gradient/down: So its negative points the way the loss falls fastest: exactly where the blindfolded hiker wants to step.
numerical/recipe: The definition of the slope hands us an algorithm: nudge a weight by a small h, and see how much the loss changes.
numerical/loop: Here it is in code. Loop over every single weight.
numerical/nudge: Nudge it up by h, and evaluate the loss. Nudge it down by h, and evaluate again.
numerical/back: Then put the weight back exactly the way it was.
numerical/div: The change in loss, divided by the total run of two h, is the slope for that one weight.
numerical/fill: One weight at a time, the gradient fills in.
numerical/centered: Nudging both ways is called the centered difference. Why not nudge just one way, like the textbook definition?
numerical/lean: A one sided step measures the slope over a stretch that runs off to one side. If the curve bends, the estimate leans.
numerical/cancel: The centered stretch is balanced, so the leaning from the two sides cancels. Its error shrinks like h squared, instead of like h.
tiny-h/small: So how small should h be? Here is the error of both recipes, for every h from one down to ten to the minus twelve.
tiny-h/fall: As h shrinks, the error falls, and twice as steeply for the centered recipe.
tiny-h/rise: But keep going, and it climbs back up. At a tiny h, the two losses agree in almost every digit, so their difference is mostly rounding noise.
tiny-h/sweet: The centered difference does best near ten to the minus five, which is exactly the course's advice.
tiny-h/f32: In single precision, which GPUs favor, the sweet spot moves to a larger h, and the best error is far worse. So gradient checks use double precision.
tiny-h/slow: Numerical gradients are simple and always available. But they are approximate, and slow.
tiny-h/cost: Two loss evaluations per weight: for see-far ten, sixty one thousand four hundred and sixty passes over the training set, for a single step.
tiny-h/better: And a modern network has millions of weights. We need something better.
analytic/formula: The better way: derive a formula for the gradient with calculus, once, on paper, then just evaluate it. Exact, and about as cheap as the loss.
analytic/catch: The catch is that a hand derived formula is easy to get subtly wrong. So the numerical gradient stays around, as a check.
analytic/one: Take the SVM loss of one example. For each wrong class j, a hinge: the max of zero, and that class's score minus the correct score, plus one.
analytic/fact1: Two facts are all we need. First, the hinge. Its slope is zero on the flat part, and one on the ramp.
analytic/fact2: Second, a score is a row of weights dotted with x. Raise one weight by one, and the score rises by the matching input. So its slope, with respect to the row, is x itself.
analytic/multiply: Multiply the outer slope by the inner one. That is the chain rule, the star of the next chapter.
analytic/wrong: For a wrong class j: if it violates the margin, the gradient for its row is x. If not, it is zero.
analytic/right: The correct class's score enters every active hinge with a minus sign. So its row gets minus x, once for each violator.
analytic/picture: Here is what that does in a toy problem. Each thick arrow is one row of W, one class's weights. The dashed line is one example, x.
analytic/push: Stepping against the gradient pushes each violating row away from x, lowering that wrong score.
analytic/pull: And it pulls the correct row toward x, raising the right score. Exactly the fix we want.
analytic/step: Take a few steps, and watch the margins in the code shrink.
analytic/full: For the full loss, average these over the training set, and add two lambda W from the penalty.
check/both: So in practice we compute both, and compare. This is a gradient check, and the assignment has you run one.
check/rel: It uses the relative error: the size of the difference, divided by the size of the larger of the two.
check/why: A gap of one thousandth is alarming between gradients near two thousandths, and meaningless near a thousand. Dividing by their size gives one yardstick.
check/good: In double precision, a correct gradient usually shows a relative error around ten to the minus seven, or smaller.
check/bad: Above about ten to the minus two, it almost always means a bug: a flipped sign, or a forgotten term.
check/crease: A kinked loss like the SVM can show a larger error when a nudge happens to cross a crease. That one is not a bug.
check/table: The numerical gradient is slow, approximate, and hard to get wrong. The analytic gradient is fast, exact, and easy to get wrong.
check/use: Use the analytic one for training, and the numerical one to check it.
descent/simple: With the gradient in hand, the procedure is almost embarrassingly simple.
descent/loop: Compute the gradient. Take a small step against it. Repeat.
descent/why: Why small? The gradient only says which way is downhill right here. A little further on, the ground may tilt differently.
descent/eta: How far to step is set by the step size, eta, or learning rate: the most important knob in training a network.
descent/valley: Watch it on a long, narrow valley: steep across, nearly flat along. Real loss landscapes are full of these.
descent/crawl: With a tiny step size, the path creeps. After sixty steps, it is still far from the bottom.
descent/smooth: Around zero point zero five, it drops into the valley, and glides along the floor to the bottom.
descent/zigzag: Bigger, and it overshoots the steep direction on every step, zig-zagging from wall to wall, though the bounces shrink.
descent/diverge: Bigger still, and every bounce is larger than the last. The loss explodes.
descent/thresh: This valley is ten times steeper across. Past a step size of zero point one, the path zig-zags. Past zero point two, it diverges.
descent/limit: The steep direction sets the speed limit for every direction. That is why narrow valleys are slow.
descent/tune: There is no formula for the right step size. You find it by experiment.
minibatch/avg: One last problem. The loss averages over the whole training set, and so does its gradient: computing it exactly means visiting every example, every step.
minibatch/imagenet: For the ImageNet challenge, with one point two million training images, that is extremely wasteful.
minibatch/batch: The fix: estimate the gradient from a small random sample, a mini-batch. Say, two hundred and fifty six images out of the one point two million.
minibatch/code: Each step draws a fresh batch, computes the gradient on just those examples, and steps.
minibatch/poll: Like a poll of a few hundred voters standing in for a whole country, it is right on average, and close most of the time.
minibatch/trade: It is a little noisy, but thousands of times cheaper: thousands of wobbly steps in the time of one perfect one.
minibatch/race: Back on our slice: full batch, in teal, uses all three hundred points per step. Mini-batch, in orange, uses four. It wobbles, but heads the same way.
minibatch/work: Now count the work. For any number of examples looked at, the mini-batch run is far ahead.
minibatch/redundant: Why does it work so well? Partly because data is redundant. Imagine the one point two million images were copies of just a thousand.
minibatch/copies: Then the gradient from those thousand would equal the full one exactly. Real data is not that redundant, but redundant enough.
minibatch/pow: Batch sizes are usually powers of two, like thirty two or two hundred and fifty six, mostly set by what fits in memory.
minibatch/sgd: With a batch of one, it is called stochastic gradient descent, or SGD. In practice, people say SGD for mini-batches too.
summary/four: Putting it all together: four pieces make the whole training loop.
summary/score: A score function maps an input to class scores.
summary/loss: A loss function grades those scores with one number.
summary/grad: The gradient says which way is uphill for every weight: analytic for speed, numerical to check.
summary/update: And the update steps the weights downhill, usually one mini-batch at a time.
summary/rest: The rest of the course plugs into this loop. Neural networks swap in a richer score function, and the loop stays the same.
summary/hard: What changes is the gradient. Deriving it by hand, as we did for the SVM, would be hopeless for a deep network.
summary/backprop: The next chapter introduces backpropagation: the chain rule, applied piece by piece, to get the gradient of anything built from simple parts.
summary/recap: So: training is optimization. The loss is a landscape, the gradient points uphill, and we step against it, one mini-batch at a time.
